'''Antoni Szczepan Zygmund''' ({{IPA|pl|anˈtɔɲi ˈzɘgmunt}}; 26 December 1900<ref>{{Britannica|title=Antoni Zygmund|author=The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica}}</ref> – 30 May 1992) was a Polish-American [[mathematician]]. He worked mostly in the area of [[mathematical analysis]], including [[harmonic analysis]], and he is considered one of the greatest analysts of the 20th century.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/04/20/us/alberto-calderon-77-pioneer-of-mathematical-analysis.html|title=Alberto Calderon, 77, Pioneer Of Mathematical Analysis|last=Noble|first=Holcomb B.|date=1998-04-20|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-06-23|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1998-04-19-9804190439-story.html|title=ALBERTO CALDERON, MATH GENIUS|last=Warnick|first=Mark S.|website=chicagotribune.com|date=19 April 1998 |language=en-US|access-date=2019-06-23}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Zygmund.html|title=Antoni Zygmund (1900-1992)|website=www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk|access-date=2019-06-23}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1998/04/20/professor-alberto-calderon-77-dies/069850e0-284c-4f03-9ce8-64a7e114274c/|title=PROFESSOR ALBERTO CALDERON, 77, DIES|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=2019-06-22|language=en-US|issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref name="Lorentz">{{cite journal|author=Lorentz, G. G.|title=Antoni Zygmund and His Work|journal=[[Journal of Approximation Theory]]|year=1993|volume=75|pages=1–7|doi=10.1006/jath.1993.1084|url=https://history-of-approximation-theory.com/fpapers/zygmund_work.pdf|doi-access=free}}</ref> Zygmund was responsible for creating the [[Chicago school (mathematical analysis)|Chicago school of mathematical analysis]] together with his doctoral student [[Alberto Calderón]], for which he was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]], the highest American science award, in 1986.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

==Life and career==
Zygmund was born on 26 December 1900 in [[Warsaw]], then part of the [[Russian Empire]], in a Polish family of Wincenty Zygmund and Antonina ({{nee|Perowska}}).<ref name="MacTut">{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Zygmund/ |title=Antoni Szczepan Zygmund |work=MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive |author= J. J. O'Connor, E. F. Robertson |access-date=6 September 2026}}</ref> He was the oldest of four siblings, with three younger sisters. In 1914, his secondary education in Warsaw was interrupted by the outbreak of [[World War I]] forcing his family to relocate to [[Poltava]] (presnet-day Ukraine). In 1918, he returned to Poland, which had just become an independent state, and spent a year studying at Kazimierz Kulwiee’s [[Gymnasium (school)|Gymnasium]] in Warsaw.<ref name="MacTut" />

The following year, he enrolled at the [[University of Warsaw]]<ref name="Wójcik" /> and studied under prominent mathematicians representing the [[Warsaw School of Mathematics]] including [[Zygmunt Janiszewski]], [[Stefan Mazurkiewicz]] and [[Wacław Sierpiński]].<ref name="Bójko">{{cite web|url=https://wyborcza.pl/AkcjeSpecjalne/7,160474,24678902,po-co-nam-sinus-i-cosinus.html |language=pl |title=Po co ci sinus? Poznaj Antoniego Zygmunda - matematyka, bez którego świat wyglądałby inaczej |trans-title=Why Do You Need Sine? Meet Antoni Zygmund - A Mathematician Without Whom the World Would Look Very Different |work=Gazeta Wyborcza |author=Marcin Bójko |date=19 April 2019 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> In 1920, Zygmund’s education was interrupted again when he was drafted into the army. He did not take part in active combat in the [[Polish–Soviet War]] and was therefore able to resume his academic work. During his time at the University of Warsaw, Zygmund was particularly influenced by [[Aleksander Rajchman]], attending his lectures and a seminar on the theory of [[trigonometric series]]. In 1923, Zygmund obtained his [[doctorate]] from the University of Warsaw based on his thesis concerning the Riemannian theory of trigonometric series written under the formal supervision of Mazurkiewicz.<ref name="MacTut" /><ref name="Bójko" />

In 1922–26, Zygmund worked as an assistant at the [[Warsaw University of Technology]]. In 1926, he earned his [[habilitation]] and assumed the position of a [[docent]] at the University of Warsaw. In 1929, he was granted a [[Rockefeller Foundation]] scholarship<ref name="CelMath" /> and spent a year in [[Oxford]] and [[Cambridge]], which exerted a profound impact upon his scientific development. He collaborated with such mathematicians as [[Raymond Paley]],<ref>{{cite journal | last1= Paley | first1= R. E. A. C. | last2= Zygmund | first2= Antoni | year= 1932 | title= A note on analytic functions in the unit circle | journal= Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society | volume= 28 | issue= 3 | pages= 266–272 | bibcode= 1932PCPS...28..266P | doi= 10.1017/S0305004100010112 | zbl= 0005.06602}}</ref> [[G.H. Hardy]] and [[John Edensor Littlewood|J. E. Littlewood]], publishing five joint-papers with Paley between 1930 and 1931.<ref name="Wójcik" /><ref name="MacTut" />

In 1935, Zygmund published in Polish the original edition of what has become, in its English translation, the two-volume ''[[Trigonometric Series]]''. It was described by Robert A. Fefferman as "one of the most influential books in the history of mathematical analysis" and "an extraordinarily comprehensive and masterful presentation of a ... vast field".<ref name="Zygmund Fefferman">The 2nd edition of Zygmund's ''Trigonometric Series'' ([[Cambridge University Press]], 1959) consists of 2 separate volumes. The 3rd edition (Cambridge University Press, 2002, {{ISBN|0 521 89053 5}}) consists of the two volumes combined with a foreword by Robert A. Fefferman. The nine pages in Fefferman's foreword (biographic and other information concerning Zygmund) are not numbered.</ref> [[Jean-Pierre Kahane]] called the book "The Bible" of a [[harmonic analysis|harmonic analyst]].<ref name="Lorentz"/> In 1988, a new edition of the work was published by [[Cambridge University Press]].<ref name="Saxon" /> The theory of trigonometric series had remained the largest component of Zygmund's mathematical investigations.<ref name="Lorentz"/>

Zygmund also worked with [[Stanisław Saks]], with whom he co-authored the book ''Analytic Functions'' published in the ''Monografie Matematyczne'' (Mathematical Monographs) series in 1938.<ref name="Wójcik">{{cite web|url=https://gigancinauki.pl/gn/biogramy/83777,Zygmund-Antoni-Szczepan.html |language=pl |title=Zygmund Antoni Szczepan |website=gigancinauki.pl |author=Wiesław Wójcik |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>

Zygmund was a professor at [[Vilnius University|Stefan Batory University]] in [[Vilnius|Wilno]] from 1930 to 1939. During this period,  he began a highly productive scientific collaboration with his most gifted student, [[Józef Marcinkiewicz]], with whom he also developed a close personal friendship. Together they obtained significant results in [[real analysis|real]] and [[Fourier analysis]], [[probability theory]], and moment inequalities, contributions that later became foundational in several areas of modern mathematical analysis.<ref name="WybBog">{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=54VF6nzHKg8&t=3783s |title=Wybraniec bogów -fabularyzowany film dokumentalny [English subtitles] |trans-title=Gods' Chosen One: A Dramatzed Documentary Film |website=YouTube |publisher=IPNtvPL |date=22 April 2022 |access-date=8 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://norbertwiener.umd.edu/NW/Marcinkiewicz_Bio_2.pdf |title=Józef Marcinkiewicz–his life and work |work=norbertwiener.umd.edu |author=Roman Sznajder |date=19 March 2019 |access-date=8 September 2026}}</ref> Zygmund also further developed many of Marcinkiewicz's ideas after his student's tragic death and played an important role in helping preserve his scientific legacy abroad.<ref name="Wójcik" /><ref name="WybBog" />

[[File:Harper_Midway_Chicago.jpg|thumb|Zygmund spent most of his academic career at the [[University of Chicago]]]]

When [[World War II]] broke out, Poland was [[Occupation of Poland (1939–1945)|occupied]] and,  in 1940, Zygmund managed to emigrate to the [[United States]]. Thanks to the support from [[Jerzy Neyman]], [[Jacob Tamarkin]] and [[Norbert Wiener]], he received an invitation to [[Mount Holyoke College]] in [[South Hadley, Massachusetts]] where he became a professor.<ref name="Wójcik" /> In 1945–1947, he was a professor at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], and from 1947, until his retirement, at the [[University of Chicago]]. During his time in Chicago, Zygmund together with his student [[Alberto Calderon]] (whom he had met in 1948 in Argentina),<ref name="Bójko" /> founded the [[Chicago school of mathematical analysis]], a [[school of thought]] in mathematics that highlights the use of Fourier analysis in the study of [[partial differential equations]]. It became one of the most influential analytical schools of the 20th century, contributing many of the field’s major advances.<ref name="Holcomb">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/04/20/us/alberto-calderon-77-pioneer-of-mathematical-analysis.html|title=Alberto Calderon, 77, Pioneer Of Mathematical Analysis|last=Noble|first=Holcomb B.|date=1998-04-20|work=The New York Times|access-date=8 September 2026|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name="Warnick">{{Cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1998-04-19-9804190439-story.html|title=ALBERTO CALDERON, MATH GENIUS|last=Warnick|first=Mark S.|website=chicagotribune.com|date=19 April 1998 |language=en-US|access-date=8 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="CalD">{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1998/04/20/professor-alberto-calderon-77-dies/069850e0-284c-4f03-9ce8-64a7e114274c/|title=PROFESSOR ALBERTO CALDERON, 77, DIES|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=8 September 2026|language=en-US|issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

He was a member of several scientific societies. From 1930 until 1952 he was a member of the [[Warsaw Scientific Society]] (''TNW''), from 1946 of the [[Polish Academy of Learning]] (''PAU''), from 1959 of the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] (''PAN''), and from 1961 of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in the United States.<ref name="MacTut" />

In 1954, Zygmund participated as an invited speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in [[Amsterdam]].<ref name="CelMath">{{cite web|url=https://celebratio.org/Zygmund_A/article/403/ |title=Antoni Zygmund |work=Celebratio Mathematica |author=Editorial Committee of Studia Mathematica |date=1992 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>

In 1979, Zygmund was awarded the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]] from the [[American Mathematical Society]] for "his cumulative influence on the theory of [[Fourier series]], [[real variables]], and related areas of analysis."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/prizes-awards/pabrowse.cgi?parent_id=28 |title=Leroy P. Steele Prize (1970 - 1992) |work=American Mathematical Society |access-date=8 September 2026}}</ref>

In 1986, Zygmund received the [[National Medal of Science]], the highest science award in the United States,<ref>{{Cite web |title=About the National Medal of Science |url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/special_reports/medalofscience50/about.jsp |access-date=2026-09-06 |website=www.nsf.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-09-11 |title=President Biden awards National Medal of Science to Brown engineer Subra Suresh |url=https://www.brown.edu/news/2023-10-24/suresh-medal-science |access-date=2026-09-06 |website=www.brown.edu |language=en}}</ref> from [[President of the United States|President]] [[Ronald Reagan]] for his outstanding contribution to the development of Fourier analysis, as well as its application to partial differential equations and other branches of [[mathematical analysis]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://naukawpolsce.pl/aktualnosci/news%2C33102%2Cprof-strzelecki-antoni-zygmund-zdobywca-matematycznych-himalajow.html |language=pl |title=Prof. Strzelecki: Antoni Zygmund to zdobywca matematycznych Himalajów |trans-title=Prof. Strzelecki: Antoni Zygmund is the Conquerer of the Mathematical Himalayas |website=naukawpolsce.pl |author=Ludwika Tomala |date=10 March 2019 |access-date=8 September 2026}}</ref> He was also recognized for his "creation and leadership of the strongest school of analytical research in the contemporary mathematical world."<ref name="MacTut" /><ref name="Holcomb" /><ref name="Warnick" /><ref name="CalD" />

In 1981, he was granted emeritus status.<ref name="Saxon" /> Zygmund continued attending analysis seminars at Chicago even in his eighties, contributing profound and incisive insights.<ref name="Carbery" /> He died on 30 May 1992 in Chicago, at the age of 91.<ref name="Saxon">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/06/03/us/antoni-zygmund-91-professor-of-mathematics-in-chicago-dies.html |title=Antoni Zygmund, 91, Professor Of Mathematics in Chicago, Dies |work=The New York Times  |author=Wolfgang Saxon |date=3 June 1992 |access-date=8 September 2026}}</ref>

Zygmund published six books and more than 180 scientific papers during his career.<ref name="Saxon" /> He was the advisor of 40 doctoral students, including [[Alberto Calderón]], [[Paul Cohen]] ([[Fields Medal]] winner), [[Nathan Fine]], [[Józef Marcinkiewicz]], [[Victor L. Shapiro]], [[Guido Weiss]], [[Elias M. Stein]] and [[Mischa Cotlar]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=6388 |title=Antoni Zygmund |work=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=8 September 2026}}</ref>

==Contributions==
His work has had a pervasive influence in many fields of mathematics, mostly in mathematical analysis, and particularly in [[harmonic analysis]]. Among his chief interests in that area was expressing vibrating bodies in precise mathematical terms, a key issue in [[aerospace engineering|spacecraft engineering]], [[crystallography]], and [[holography|laser holography]].<ref name="Saxon" />

Some of his most important contributions concerned the theory of [[singular integrals|singular integral operators]], and were achieved in collaboration with Calderón.<ref name="Carbery">{{cite news|title=Obituary: Professor Antoni Zygmund|author=Carbery, Tony|newspaper=The Independent|date=17 July 1992|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-professor-antoni-zygmund-1533716.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220507/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-professor-antoni-zygmund-1533716.html |archive-date=2022-05-07 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Zygmund Fefferman"/> In particular, the [[Calderón–Zygmund lemma]] is regarded as a fundamental result in this area of mathematics. It was developed to prove the weak-type continuity of singular integrals of [[integrable function]]s becoming a standard tool in analysis and [[probability theory]]. [[George G. Lorentz]] called it Zygmund's crowning achievement, one that "stands somewhat apart from the rest of Zygmund's work".<ref name="Lorentz"/>

Zygmund, together with [[Raphaël Salem]], demonstrated that a [[Cantor set|Cantor-like set]] with dissection ratio ξ is a [[set of uniqueness]] if and only if 1/ξ is a [[Pisot–Vijayaraghavan number|Pisot number]], that is an [[algebraic integer]] characterized by the fact that all its [[Conjugate element (field theory)|conjugates]] (if any) are smaller than 1. Their result was the first to show that the uniqueness property depends on arithmetic features rather than merely on notions of size.<ref>{{cite book
| last= Bertin | first= M. J. | author2= Decomps-Guilloux, A. | author3= Grandet-Hugot, M. | author4= Pathiaux-Delefosse, M. | author5= Schreiber, J. P. | year= 1992 | chapter= The Salem–Zygmund Theorem | title= Pisot and Salem Numbers | publisher  =Birkhäuser | location= Basel | doi= 10.1007/978-3-0348-8632-1_15}}</ref>

The [[Marcinkiewicz–Zygmund inequality]] is another significant result by Zygmund. It establishes relationships between the [[Moment (mathematics)|moments]] of [[Independence (probability theory)|independent random variables]] and constitutes a generalization of the rule for the sum of [[variance]]s of independent random variables to moments of arbitrary order.

Other concepts named after Zygmund include the [[Paley–Zygmund inequality]],<ref>{{cite journal | last= Ghosh | first= B. K. | year= 2002 | title= Probability inequalities related to Markov's theorem | journal= The American Statistician | volume= 56 | issue= 3 | pages= 186–190 | doi= 10.1198/000313002119 | jstor= 3087296 | mr= 1940206 | s2cid= 120451773}}</ref> [[Calderón–Zygmund kernel]], [[Calderón–Zygmund decomposition]] and [[Singular integral#Singular integrals of non-convolution type|Calderón–Zygmund operators]].

==Family==
Antoni Zygmund, who had three sisters, married Irena Parnowska, a mathematician, in 1925.<ref name=":2"/> Upon his death he was survived by four grandsons.<ref>{{cite news|title=Obituary. Antoni Zygmund, 91, U. of C. Math Professor|date=June 2, 1992|newspaper=Chicago Tribune|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1992/06/02/antoni-zygmund-91-u-of-c-math-professor/}}</ref>

==Awards and recognition==
Zygmund received a number of awards and distinctions, some of which include:<ref name=MacTut />

*1953: [[Guggenheim Fellowship]]<ref name="CelMath" />
*1954: Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]]<ref name="CelMath" />
*1959: Member of the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] 
*1961: Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]]
*1964: Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences of Argentina]]
*1967: Member of the [[Royal Academy of Exact, Physical and Natural Sciences|Spanish Royal Academy of Sciences]],  the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and the  [[London Mathematical Society]]
*1972: [[Jurzykowski Prize|Jurzykowski Foundation Prize]], member of the [[Polish Mathematical Society]]
*1979: [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]]
*1986: [[National Medal of Science]]

He accepted [[honorary doctorate]]s from [[Mount Holyoke College]], [[Washington University]], the [[Nicolaus Copernicus University]] in [[Toruń]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.umk.pl/o-uczelni/historia-i-liczby/wyroznienia-uniwersyteckie/doktorzy-honoris-causa/ |language=pl |title=Doktorzy honoris causa |trans-title=Honorary Doctorates  |work=Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń |access-date=8 September 2026}}</ref> the [[University of Paris]], and the [[University of Uppsala]].<ref name=MacTut />

==Books==
*''Trigonometric Series'' (Cambridge University Press 1959, 2002)
*''Intégrales singulières'' ([[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]], 1971)
*''Trigonometric Interpolation'' (University of Chicago, 1950)
*''Measure and Integral: An Introduction to Real Analysis'', with Richard L. Wheeden ([[Marcel Dekker]], 1977)
*''Analytic Functions'', with [[Stanislaw Saks]] ([[Elsevier]] Science Ltd, 1971)
